title: Pulmonary Hypertension
subject: Pathology
summary: Pulmonary hypertension is a haemodynamic disorder with mean pulmonary arterial pressure ≥ 20 mmHg at rest. It results from vascular remodeling, left‑heart disease, lung disease, chronic thrombo‑embolism or multifactorial causes and leads to right‑heart failure.

sections.p: PH is defined by a mean pulmonary arterial pressure (mPAP) ≥ 20 mmHg measured by right‑heart catheterisation (RHC). The diagnosis requires exclusion of acute causes and confirmation of chronic elevation.
b: RHC is the gold standard; echocardiography is the bedside screen.
mPAP ≥ 20 mmHg, pulmonary capillary wedge pressure ≤ 15 mmHg for pre‑capillary PH.

t.b: Does the patient have elevated right‑systolic pressure? A tricuspid regurgitant jet ≥ 3.4 m/s suggests mPAP ≥ 20 mmHg.
What is the exact haemodynamic profile? Confirms mPAP, pulmonary vascular resistance (PVR) and wedge pressure; required before targeted therapy.
Is there evidence of pulmonary artery enlargement or right‑heart enlargement? Supports PH but is non‑specific.

sections.p: Severity is graded by WHO functional class (I–IV) and by haemodynamics (PVR, cardiac output). Staging guides therapy intensity.
b: WHO‑FC I: No limitation of ordinary activity.
WHO‑FC IV: Symptoms at rest, signs of right‑heart failure.

t.b: How limited is exercise capacity? Distance < 300 m indicates severe disease.
Is right‑ventricular strain present? Levels > 300 pg/mL correlate with worse prognosis.

sections.p: In low‑resource East African settings, the most common contributors are chronic lung disease, left‑heart disease, and infections that affect the pulmonary vasculature.
b: Group 1 (PAH): HIV, connective‑tissue disease, congenital shunts.
Group 2: Rheumatic mitral stenosis, hypertensive heart disease.
Group 3: COPD, post‑TB fibrosis, chronic hypoxia from high altitude.
Group 4: Chronic thrombo‑embolic PH (CTEPH) after untreated VTE.
Group 5: Schistosomiasis, sickle‑cell disease, herbal toxins.

sections.p: Patients develop progressive dyspnoea, fatigue and peripheral oedema. Early disease may show disproportionate dyspnoea compared with spirometry.
b: Exertional dyspnoea out of proportion to lung function.
Loud P2, right‑sided S3, jugular venous distension.
Ankle swelling, hepatomegaly in advanced stages.

sections.p: A stepwise approach uses bedside tools first, then referral for definitive haemodynamic measurement.
b: Echocardiography to estimate pressure and assess right‑ventricular size.
Chest imaging to look for lung disease or pulmonary artery enlargement.
Pulmonary function tests (PFTs) to differentiate lung‑ versus heart‑origin.

t.b: Is there obstructive or restrictive lung disease? Normal FEV1/FVC with low DLCO suggests vascular disease.
Is chronic thrombo‑embolism present? Mismatched perfusion defects point to CTEPH.
Is HIV a contributing factor? Positive result moves patient to Group 1 PAH.
Is schistosomiasis present? Positive serology supports Group 5 PH in endemic areas.

sections.p: Uncontrolled PH rapidly leads to right‑heart failure and death.
b: Sudden worsening dyspnoea with syncope – possible acute decompensation.
Peripheral cyanosis, hypotension – impending right‑ventricular collapse.
Recurrent haemoptysis – may signal pulmonary artery rupture.

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then add targeted therapy and supportive measures.
b: Oxygen therapy for chronic hypoxia (PaO2 < 55 mmHg or 7.3 kPa).
Diuretics for right‑sided fluid overload.
Anticoagulation if CTEPH or recurrent VTE is confirmed.
Endothelin‑receptor antagonists (e.g., bosentan) for Group 1 PAH – reduce vasoconstriction.
Phosphodiesterase‑5 inhibitors (e.g., sildenafil) – improve nitric‑oxide pathway.
Avoid calcium‑channel blockers unless vasoreactivity test is positive.

sections.p: Regular clinical review, functional class assessment and repeat echocardiography guide therapy escalation.
b: Clinic review every 3–6 months; earlier if symptoms change.
Repeat 6MWT and NT‑proBNP to track progression.
Vaccinate against influenza and pneumococcus to reduce respiratory infections.
Left‑sided heart failure – both cause dyspnoea, but left‑sided failure shows pulmonary crackles and elevated wedge pressure.
Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease – COPD has obstructive spirometry and smoking history; PH has normal spirometry early.
Pulmonary embolism – acute onset, pleuritic chest pain, and CT pulmonary angiography differentiate.
Normal echocardiographic pressure estimate in early disease – RHC may still reveal elevated mPAP.
Low NT‑proBNP in obese patients – may mask right‑ventricular strain.
Chest X‑ray may appear normal despite severe PH.

whenToSeekHelp: Rapid increase in leg swelling with abdominal distension

faq.q: Why is right‑heart catheterisation required before starting PAH‑specific drugs?
faq.a: It confirms the haemodynamic definition, distinguishes pre‑ from post‑capillary PH and avoids treating left‑heart disease with inappropriate vasodilators.

faq.q: Can long‑term oxygen therapy improve survival?
faq.a: Yes, in chronic hypoxic PH it reduces pulmonary vasoconstriction and improves survival when used ≥15 hours daily.

faq.q: Is PH curable in low‑resource settings?
faq.a: Cure is rare; control of the underlying cause (e.g., treating HIV, repairing a shunt) and symptom management can markedly improve quality of life.

exam: A 35‑year‑old woman with HIV presents with exertional dyspnoea; echo shows TR jet 3.6 m/s. What is the next diagnostic step and why? — Right‑heart catheterisation to confirm pre‑capillary PH and guide therapy.

A patient with rheumatic mitral stenosis develops PH. How does the underlying mechanism differ from PAH? — Elevated left‑atrial pressure raises wedge pressure (post‑capillary PH), so vasodilators are contraindicated.
In a rural clinic you cannot perform RHC. Which bedside test helps risk‑stratify and what threshold indicates severe disease? — 6‑minute walk distance <300 m suggests severe PH.
Why is a calcium‑channel blocker not first‑line for most PH patients? — Only a small subset shows acute vasoreactivity; indiscriminate use can cause systemic hypotension.
A patient on sildenafil develops worsening oedema. What should you do? — Review for right‑heart failure; add diuretic and consider switching to an endothelin‑receptor antagonist.

How does chronic schistosomiasis cause PH and what specific investigation confirms it? — Egg‑induced portal hypertension leads to pulmonary vascular remodeling; serology or stool microscopy confirms infection.
What red‑flag symptom mandates immediate hospital admission in PH? — New syncope or rapid progression of right‑sided heart failure signs.

Explain why anticoagulation is recommended in chronic thrombo‑embolic PH but not in isolated PAH. — CTEPH involves persistent thrombus; anticoagulation prevents further emboli, whereas PAH risk of bleeding outweighs benefit.

sections.h: Bedside: history and how to examine
sections.p: A focused history and systematic exam can differentiate pre‑capillary from post‑capillary PH, identify the likely WHO group and detect early right‑ventricular failure, even where advanced imaging is unavailable.
b: Onset and progression of dyspnoea (gradual vs acute).
Exertional limitation: WHO‑FC I‑IV clues.
Syncope or presyncope episodes.
Peripheral oedema, abdominal distension, weight gain.
Chest pain or palpitations (right‑sided arrhythmia).
Risk factors: HIV, schistosomiasis, TB, rheumatic heart disease, COPD, high‑altitude residence, intravenous drug use, pregnancy.
Medication and herbal toxin exposure (e.g., appetite suppressants, fenfluramine).
Family history of PAH or congenital heart disease.

t.b: Detects elevated right atrial pressure; visible pulsation >3 cm above the sternal angle indicates right‑sided overload. Cannot quantify pressure.
Grade 2+ or higher supports systemic congestion; does not distinguish PH from other causes of fluid overload.

t.a: Abdominal exam for hepatomegaly and ascites (shifting dullness)
t.b: Hepatomegaly >2 cm below costal margin and shifting dullness confirm right‑heart failure; cannot assess portal hypertension severity.

t.a: Six‑minute walk test (6‑MWD) performed in a corridor
t.b: Measures functional capacity; distance <165 m denotes high‑risk PH. Not a substitute for haemodynamics.

t.a: Bedside acute vasoreactivity test with inhaled nitric oxide (if available)
t.b: A drop in mean PAP ≥10 mmHg to ≤40 mmHg with unchanged/increased CO defines a positive test; not feasible in most low‑resource settings.

sections.h: Investigations and how to read them
sections.p: Use a stepwise algorithm: bedside echo → chest X‑ray/PFT → targeted labs → referral for right‑heart catheterisation (RHC) when possible. Each test answers a specific clinical question.
b: Echocardiography: estimates systolic PAP, assesses RV size/function, looks for left‑heart disease.
Chest X‑ray: pulmonary artery enlargement, lung parenchymal disease, pleural effusion.
Pulmonary function tests (spirometry + DLCO): differentiate obstructive, restrictive, or isolated diffusion defect.
Ventilation‑perfusion (V/Q) scan: screens for chronic thrombo‑embolic PH.
CT pulmonary angiography: confirms CTEPH or parenchymal disease when V/Q unavailable.
Laboratory panel: HIV serology, hepatitis, schistosomiasis serology, BNP/NT‑proBNP, complete blood count, renal & liver function.
Right‑heart catheterisation (RHC): gold‑standard haemodynamics.

t.b: Answers: estimated systolic PAP. Calculate PAP = 4 × (TR velocity)² + RAP (estimated 5–10 mmHg). TR velocity ≥3.4 m/s suggests severe PH. Cannot replace RHC.
Answers: RV dilation. RV basal diameter >42 mm (or RV/LV >1) indicates RV overload. Does not give pressure values.
Answers: pulmonary vascular resistance estimate. PAAT <100 ms suggests elevated PVR. Not precise without RHC.
Answers: distinguishes PAH (often low DLCO) from lung disease (DLCO proportionate to FVC). A DLCO <60 % predicted supports pre‑capillary PH.
Answers: presence of mismatched perfusion defects. Multiple segmental defects → high suspicion for CTEPH; normal scan makes CTEPH unlikely.
Answers: risk stratification. >1400 pg/mL (or >600 pg/mL without comorbidities) denotes high‑risk PH. Not diagnostic alone.
Answers: identifies calcium‑channel blocker responders. Positive if mean PAP drops ≥10 mmHg to ≤40 mmHg with unchanged/increased CO and no systemic hypotension.

t.a: Serum‑ascites albumin gradient (SAAG) if ascites present
t.b: Answers: distinguishes portal hypertension (SAAG ≥1.1 g/dL) from exudative causes. High SAAG supports right‑heart failure‑related ascites.

sections.p: Combine clinical, imaging and haemodynamic data to place the patient into a WHO group, assign functional class and grade severity for prognostication and treatment decisions.
b: Post‑capillary PH: mPAP ≥20 mmHg, PCWP >15 mmHg; isolated post‑capillary when PVR ≤3 WU, combined when PVR >3 WU.
WHO functional class I–IV based on symptom limitation.
High‑risk criteria (any): WHO‑FC IV, 6‑MWD <165 m, NT‑proBNP >1400 pg/mL, RAP >14 mmHg, cardiac index <2.0 L/min/m², TR velocity >3.4 m/s.
Intermediate‑risk: meets 1–2 high‑risk criteria; low‑risk: none of the above.
Group allocation: 1 PAH (e.g., HIV, CTD), 2 left‑heart disease, 3 lung disease/hypoxia, 4 CTEPH, 5 miscellaneous (schistosomiasis, sickle cell).
Severity grading guides escalation: low‑risk → oral agents; intermediate → combination therapy; high‑risk → parenteral prostacyclin or transplant referral.

sections.p: Several diseases mimic PH signs but have distinct pathophysiology or management; a focused history and targeted investigations separate them.
b: Left‑sided heart failure: elevated PCWP, pulmonary congestion on X‑ray, normal PVR; differentiate by echo showing LV dysfunction or mitral disease.
Chronic lung disease (COPD, interstitial lung disease): obstructive/restrictive pattern on PFT, low DLCO proportionate to FVC, CT showing emphysema or fibrosis.
High‑altitude pulmonary hypertension: recent ascent, normal cardiac anatomy, resolves with descent; rule out with history and absence of structural heart disease.
Pulmonary embolism (acute): sudden dyspnoea, tachycardia, V/Q mismatch, CT angiography positive; acute PH resolves with anticoagulation.
Cor pulmonale secondary to COPD: RV hypertrophy with emphysematous changes on imaging; PVR modestly raised, not >10 WU unless advanced.

t.b: Question: Is the elevated pressure post‑capillary? Echo showing LV EF <50 % or mitral valve area <1.5 cm² confirms left‑heart cause; PCWP >15 mmHg on RHC.
Question: Is lung disease the primary driver? Spirometry with FEV1/FVC <0.7 and CT emphysema support COPD; PAH shows normal spirometry.
Question: Is there chronic thrombo‑embolic obstruction? V/Q scan with segmental mismatches or CT angiography showing organized thrombus confirms CTEPH.
Question: Is a parasitic infection present? Positive serology or stool ova for Schistosoma and hepatic peri‑portal fibrosis point to group 5.

sections.p: A structured ladder guides clinicians from bedside stabilisation to definitive disease‑modifying therapy, with clear triggers for escalation or referral in low‑resource settings.
b: First: optimise volume status – low‑dose loop diuretic, salt restriction, monitor weight and urine output.
Second: confirm pre‑capillary PH with echocardiography (TR velocity, RV size) and refer for right‑heart catheterisation when feasible.
Third: assess acute vasoreactivity; if positive, start high‑dose calcium‑channel blocker; otherwise move to oral combination therapy.
Fourth: initiate oral endothelin‑receptor antagonist (e.g., bosentan) plus phosphodiesterase‑5 inhibitor (e.g., sildenafil) for WHO‑FC II‑III patients.
Fifth: add prostacyclin pathway agent (oral selexipag or inhaled iloprost) if WHO‑FC III‑IV despite dual therapy.
Sixth: consider parenteral prostacyclin (IV epoprostenol) for high‑risk or rapidly progressive disease.
Seventh: refer for lung transplantation or atrial septostomy when refractory despite maximal therapy.

t.b: TR velocity >3.4 m/s, NT‑proBNP >1400 pg/mL, 6‑MWD <165 m, or clinical deterioration despite dual oral therapy.
Calcium‑channel blockers without a positive vasoreactivity test; indiscriminate combination of three oral agents without specialist input; high‑dose diuretics causing renal hypoperfusion.

sections.h: Drug effects and what to do
sections.p: Recognise the most common adverse events of PH‑specific agents and manage them promptly to maintain adherence and prevent harm.
b: Endothelin‑receptor antagonists: hepatic transaminase rise – obtain baseline LFTs, repeat monthly, stop if >3× ULN.
Phosphodiesterase‑5 inhibitors: visual disturbances, headache – counsel, reduce dose if severe, avoid nitrates.
Prostacyclin analogues: infusion site pain, thrombocytopenia – rotate sites, monitor platelets, treat pain with NSAIDs if no contraindication.
Calcium‑channel blockers: hypotension, edema – monitor BP, consider diuretic, discontinue if systolic <90 mmHg.

t.b: Sildenafil + nitrates → profound hypotension; avoid concurrent use.
Prefer agents without renal clearance (e.g., bosentan) and adjust diuretic dosing.

sections.p: Complications signal disease progression and dictate urgent management steps, especially in resource‑limited environments.
b: Right‑ventricular failure – peripheral edema, ascites, hepatomegaly; intensify diuretics, add aldosterone antagonist, consider inotropic support if hypotensive.
Syncope or near‑syncope – high‑risk; admit, reassess haemodynamics, expedite prostacyclin initiation.
Hemoptysis – evaluate for pulmonary artery rupture; hold anticoagulation, consider bronchial artery embolisation.
Thromboembolic events – suspect CTEPH; obtain ventilation‑perfusion scan, refer for surgical/endovascular evaluation.

t.b: Any high‑risk sign (TR >3.4 m/s, NT‑proBNP >1400 pg/mL, 6‑MWD <165 m) or clinical decompensation mandates referral to PH centre.
New or worsening right‑heart failure, syncope, massive hemoptysis, or rapid rise in mPAP on repeat echo.

sections.p: Co‑morbidities common in East Africa modify presentation, test interpretation and therapeutic choices.
b: HIV infection – may cause PAH; CD4 count influences drug safety; avoid endothelin antagonists with severe liver disease from co‑infection.
Active TB – pulmonary infiltrates mimic PH; treat TB first, delay prostacyclin until infection controlled.
Malnutrition – low albumin alters drug binding; monitor for edema, adjust diuretic dose.
Pregnancy – PAH mortality high; avoid teratogenic agents (e.g., endothelin antagonists), use prostacyclin infusion if needed.
Renal failure – limit phosphodiesterase‑5 inhibitors if eGFR <30 mL/min; monitor fluid balance closely.
Hepatic dysfunction – endothelin antagonists contraindicated if transaminases >3× ULN; use sildenafil cautiously.

t.b: Traditional plant extracts may contain hepatotoxins; obtain thorough medication history, check LFTs before endothelin antagonists.
Exacerbates liver injury, potentiates hypotension with vasodilators; counsel on abstinence.

sections.p: Tailored strategies address the unique physiological and socioeconomic needs of vulnerable populations.
b: Children – prefer oral sildenafil and bosentan; prostacyclin infusion reserved for severe disease; monitor growth, avoid high‑dose diuretics that impair nutrition.
Pregnancy – discontinue endothelin antagonists, continue sildenafil if needed, consider IV epoprostenol; plan delivery in tertiary centre with multidisciplinary team.
Elderly – start low‑dose oral agents, watch for orthostatic hypotension, polypharmacy interactions; prioritize quality of life.
People with HIV – ensure antiretroviral therapy adherence, screen for drug‑drug interactions (e.g., protease inhibitors increase sildenafil levels).

Low‑resource settings – rely on bedside echo, NT‑proBNP, 6‑MWD for risk stratification; use affordable oral agents (sildenafil, generic bosentan), train nurses for diuretic titration, arrange periodic referral to regional PH centre.

t.b: Explain why endothelin antagonists are avoided in a pregnant woman with PAH and what alternative therapy is recommended.
Measure jugular venous pressure and assess for right‑sided S3; a JVP >10 cm H₂O suggests advanced RV failure and prompts escalation.

facts: Mean pulmonary arterial pressure ≥ 20 mmHg on right‑heart catheterisation defines pulmonary hypertension.
Pre‑capillary PH: mPAP ≥ 20 mmHg, PCWP ≤ 15 mmHg, PVR > 3 Wood units; severe when PVR > 10 Wood units.
Acute vasoreactivity test positive: fall in mPAP ≥ 10 mmHg to ≤ 40 mmHg, unchanged/increased CO, no systemic BP drop.
TR jet velocity > 3.4 m/s predicts high‑risk PH (estimated systolic PAP ≈ 4 × TR velocity² + right‑atrial pressure).
NT‑proBNP > 1400 pg/mL (or > 600 pg/mL without comorbidity) denotes high‑risk disease.
6‑minute walk distance < 165 m identifies high‑risk PH.
Add diuretic for peripheral oedema on sildenafil before changing PH‑specific therapy.

vivas.q: Define pulmonary hypertension according to current ESC/ERS criteria.
vivas.a: Mean pulmonary arterial pressure ≥ 20 mmHg measured by right‑heart catheterisation.

vivas.q: What haemodynamic profile distinguishes pre‑capillary from post‑capillary PH?
vivas.a: Pre‑capillary: PCWP ≤ 15 mmHg, PVR > 3 Wood units. Post‑capillary: PCWP > 15 mmHg.

vivas.q: List the five WHO groups and give one common cause for each in East Africa.
vivas.a: Group1 PAH – HIV; Group2 left‑heart disease – rheumatic mitral stenosis; Group3 lung disease – COPD/post‑TB fibrosis; Group4 CTEPH – untreated VTE; Group5 miscellaneous – schistosomiasis.

vivas.q: How do you perform bedside risk stratification when RHC is unavailable?
vivas.a: Use echocardiographic TR velocity, NT‑proBNP, and 6‑MWD; thresholds: TR >3.4 m/s, NT‑proBNP >1400 pg/mL, 6‑MWD <165 m.

vivas.q: Why are calcium‑channel blockers not first‑line for most PH patients?
vivas.a: Only a small vasoreactive subset (≈10%) benefits; indiscriminate use can cause systemic hypotension and worsen cardiac output.

vivas.q: A patient on sildenafil develops worsening oedema. What is the next step?
vivas.a: Add a loop diuretic, review volume status; only consider changing PH therapy if oedema persists despite diuretics.

vivas.q: Explain the pathophysiology of schistosomiasis‑associated PH and the confirmatory test.
vivas.a: Egg‑induced granulomatous inflammation of pulmonary arterioles leads to remodeling; serology for Schistosoma antibodies plus abdominal ultrasound for peri‑portal fibrosis confirms.

vivas.q: What red‑flag symptom mandates immediate admission in PH?
vivas.a: Sudden syncope or worsening dyspnoea at rest with hypotension, indicating acute right‑ventricular failure.

vivas.q: How does chronic thrombo‑embolic PH differ from idiopathic PAH regarding anticoagulation?
vivas.a: CTEPH requires lifelong anticoagulation to prevent recurrent emboli; idiopathic PAH does not have proven mortality benefit from anticoagulation.

vivas.q: Interpret a TR jet of 3.6 m/s on echo in a patient with HIV.
vivas.a: Estimated systolic PAP ≈ 4×(3.6)² ≈ 52 mmHg, indicating at least moderate PH; warrants further work‑up and referral for RHC.

vivas.q: What bedside test helps risk‑stratify PH and what threshold is used?
vivas.a: Tricuspid regurgitation velocity; >3.4 m/s signals high‑risk disease.

vivas.q: Why is inhaled nitric oxide not limited to newborns?
vivas.a: It is also used for acute vasoreactivity testing in adults and as a bridge to transplant; chronic use is not recommended.

vivas.q: Describe the physical exam sequence to detect right‑sided failure in PH.
vivas.a: Inspect for peripheral oedema, JVD; palpate RV heave; auscultate loud P2, right‑sided S3; assess hepatomegaly and ascites with percussion and fluid thrill.

vivas.q: What is the term for right‑ventricular hypertrophy and dilation caused solely by PH?
A young IV drug user presents with ARDS‑like picture; biopsy shows foreign‑body giant cell granulomas. What is the cause?
vivas.a: Talc or other particulate emboli from intravenous drug use causing foreign‑body granulomatosis and pulmonary vasculopathy.

vivas.q: What defines primary pulmonary hypertension in systemic sclerosis on RHC?
vivas.a: mPAP ≥ 20 mmHg, PCWP ≤ 15 mmHg, PVR > 3 Wood units.

vivas.q: Which oral endothelin‑1 receptor antagonist is used in systemic‑sclerosis PAH?
What is the preferred pulmonary vasodilator for persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn secondary to meconium aspiration?

mcqs.q: A 42‑year‑old woman with systemic sclerosis has an echo TR velocity of 3.5 m/s, NT‑proBNP 1500 pg/mL, and 6‑MWD 140 m. Which risk category does she belong to?
mcqs.e: All three parameters exceed high‑risk thresholds, placing her in the high‑risk category.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is NOT a typical cause of Group 3 PH in East Africa?
mcqs.e: Rheumatic mitral stenosis causes Group 2 (left‑heart) PH, not Group 3.

mcqs.q: A patient with suspected PH cannot undergo RHC. Which combination best estimates severity?
mcqs.e: Guidelines recommend TR velocity, NT‑proBNP, and 6‑minute walk distance for non‑invasive risk stratification.

mcqs.q: Which drug class is contraindicated in patients with significant left‑heart disease (Group 2 PH)?
mcqs.e: Calcium‑channel blockers can worsen left‑heart filling pressures and are avoided in Group 2 PH.

mcqs.q: Which of the following best describes cor pulmonale?
o: Right‑ventricular hypertrophy secondary to pulmonary disease
Left‑ventricular hypertrophy due to systemic hypertension
Isolated right‑atrial enlargement from tricuspid regurgitation
mcqs.e: Cor pulmonale is right‑ventricular hypertrophy and dilation caused by pulmonary hypertension.

mcqs.q: A 30‑year‑old IV drug user presents with acute dyspnoea; lung biopsy shows foreign‑body giant cell granulomas. What is the most likely aetiology?
mcqs.e: Talc or particulate emboli from contaminated injections cause foreign‑body granulomatosis and PH.

mcqs.q: Which oral agent is the first‑line endothelin‑1 receptor antagonist for systemic‑sclerosis‑associated PAH?
mcqs.e: Bosentan is the widely used oral endothelin‑1 receptor antagonist in systemic‑sclerosis PAH.

mistakes: Using a PVR >10 WU as the definition of PH rather than the severity threshold; the diagnostic cut‑off is >3 WU.
Assuming any drop in mPAP qualifies as a positive vasoreactivity test; the full criteria include absolute values and stable systemic BP.
Switching from sildenafil to an endothelin‑receptor antagonist as first response to oedema; diuretics should be added first.
Attributing foreign‑body giant cell granulomas to Pneumocystis jirovecii; the correct cause is talc or particulate emboli from IV drug use.
Relying on inhaled nitric oxide as a chronic therapy in adults; it is for acute testing/bridging, not long‑term use.
Confusing cor pulmonale with left‑sided heart failure; cor pulmonale is isolated right‑ventricular pathology due to PH.
